description: We’re a team of students interested in engineering, computer science, AI, and space exploration. We have experience in software dev, machine learning, and building projects that combine technology with real-world applications. We’re especially interested in NASA’s missions, space technology, and using AI and creative problem-solving to tackle real-world challenges. We enjoy learning new technologies, experimenting with different ideas, and finding creative ways to use our technical skills.
summary:
Cosmic Command is an interactive educational game that puts players in the role of a NASA spacecraft mission architect. Players design spacecraft, select scientific instruments, and balance engineering constraints such as mass, power, communication capabilities, and budget to complete missions across the solar system.

Our goal was to create an experience that feels like a real video game, not just an educational simulation. Through animated cutscenes, detailed graphics, cinematic launches, and progressively challenging levels, players embark on an engaging journey while learning the principles behind spacecraft engineering. The game's retro-futuristic aesthetic was inspired by NASA's restored Apollo Mission Control Center in Houston.

Built using React and TypeScript, Cosmic Command incorporates NASA-inspired mission requirements, realistic engineering constraints, and explanations of mission outcomes to demonstrate the trade-offs behind real space exploration.

By making complex aerospace concepts accessible through interactive gameplay, we hope to inspire curiosity, strengthen problem-solving skills, and introduce a new generation of students to the science and engineering that make space exploration possible.
details:
Project Overview

Cosmic Command is an interactive, browser-based educational game that simulates the process of designing and launching robotic spacecraft for NASA-inspired missions. The project was developed to address a gap in STEM education: although space exploration captures widespread public interest, the engineering principles and decision-making processes behind successful missions are often inaccessible to students without specialized technical knowledge.

Our objective was to transform spacecraft engineering into an engaging, hands-on learning experience that introduces players to scientific reasoning, systems engineering, and resource optimization. Rather than presenting technical concepts through traditional lectures or quizzes, Cosmic Command allows players to apply these principles directly by designing spacecraft, evaluating competing requirements, and observing the consequences of their decisions.

The game combines real-world NASA mission references, simplified physics-based simulations, interactive spacecraft visualization, and a retro-futuristic video game interface. We also incorporated AI-assisted development workflows, including large language models (LLMs), to support the development of more sophisticated game mechanics, technical content, and interactive features.

By making complex engineering concepts accessible through gameplay, Cosmic Command aims to encourage interest in aerospace engineering and develop transferable problem-solving skills that can be applied to challenges in energy, environmental monitoring, communications, and other technological fields.

Game Mechanics and Engineering Principles

The central gameplay revolves around five interconnected engineering decisions: spacecraft architecture, scientific instrumentation, power generation, communications, and launch vehicle selection. These categories were selected to represent the major technical considerations involved in designing a robotic space mission.

Spacecraft Architecture: Players select a flyby spacecraft, orbiter, lander, or rover based on the mission's scientific objectives. Rather than explicitly identifying the correct architecture, mission briefings require players to interpret technical requirements and determine which solution is most appropriate. This introduces requirements-based engineering, emphasizing the importance of defining a problem before selecting a technological solution.

Scientific Instrumentation: Players choose from cameras, spectrometers, radar, seismometers, drills, and thermal sensors. Each instrument contributes different scientific capabilities while increasing spacecraft mass and cost. This introduces trade-off analysis and resource optimization. It also establishes connections to Earth-observation technologies used for climate monitoring, disaster response, agricultural assessment, and environmental research.

Power Systems: Players evaluate solar panels, radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs), and batteries according to the environmental conditions of their destination. Differences in solar irradiance and operating requirements illustrate how energy availability influences spacecraft design. These concepts parallel challenges in renewable energy generation, battery storage, and the development of reliable power infrastructure.

Communication Systems: Players select communication technologies with different performance characteristics, masses, and costs. This component introduces the importance of signal transmission, communication range, and relay networks in scientific missions. The underlying principles are also relevant to satellite communications, remote connectivity, and emergency response systems.

Launch Vehicle Selection: Players choose between launch vehicles with different payload capacities and costs. Since every selected spacecraft component contributes to total mass, launch vehicle selection requires players to evaluate the cumulative consequences of earlier engineering decisions. This demonstrates systems-level optimization and the importance of resource efficiency in complex technological projects.

Throughout the design process, a continuously updated dashboard displays spacecraft mass, launch capacity, and remaining budget. Players can revise earlier decisions and immediately observe how modifications affect the overall design. This iterative workflow reflects the process of evaluating and refining engineering systems under technical and financial constraints.

Mission Structure and Progressive Learning

Cosmic Command includes four progressively challenging missions, each introducing additional engineering considerations:

- Level 1: Operation Venus Encounter

Destination: Venus

Budget: $250 million

Learning Objective: Introduction to spacecraft architecture and flyby missions.

- Level 2: Mars Mapping Initiative

Destination: Mars

Budget: $720 million

Learning Objective: Scientific instrumentation and orbital mission requirements.

- Level 3: Lunar Surface Science

Destination: Moon

Budget: $660 million

Learning Objective: Surface exploration and mobility considerations.

- Level 4: Europa Ice Explorer

Destination: Europa

Budget: $6 billion

Learning Objective: Power systems, communications, and spacecraft operation in extreme environments.

The first mission includes guided explanations that introduce the fundamental engineering concepts before players make their decisions. Subsequent missions provide increasingly complex technical briefings and require greater independent analysis.

This progression was designed to accommodate players with different levels of scientific knowledge while gradually developing their ability to solve multidisciplinary engineering problems.

The missions also demonstrate that engineering solutions are dependent on environmental and operational requirements. A system suitable for exploring the Moon may be inappropriate for a distant mission to Europa. Understanding this relationship is essential to developing adaptable technologies, whether for planetary exploration or applications on Earth.

Interactive Experience and Visual Design

A major project objective was to create an educational experience with the engagement and visual quality of a video game rather than a conventional instructional platform.

The visual design draws inspiration from NASA's restored Apollo Mission Control Center at Johnson Space Center in Houston. Retro control panels, animated displays, holographic interfaces, pixel-art characters, and cinematic transitions establish a distinctive aesthetic that connects the history of space exploration with modern interactive technology.

The game incorporates several interactive visualization systems, including a rotatable 3D spacecraft model, animated orbital trajectories, dynamically assembled spacecraft components, and a simulated rocket launch sequence.

As players select spacecraft components, the corresponding structures appear in the spacecraft visualization. The launch simulation includes a countdown, stage separation, flight telemetry, and trajectory information, allowing players to observe how engineering decisions influence mission outcomes.

These design choices serve an educational purpose beyond visual presentation. By translating abstract quantities and technical concepts into interactive representations, the interface helps students understand relationships that may be difficult to communicate through equations or written explanations alone.

The game also supports cooperative play, allowing multiple participants to assume different mission roles, including flight director, science lead, systems engineer, and communications officer. Before launch, players participate in a Flight Readiness Review in which each station must approve the spacecraft design.

This feature introduces collaborative engineering practices and emphasizes the importance of communication, interdisciplinary coordination, and shared responsibility in complex technical projects.

AI-Powered Mission Design Advisor

Cosmic Command integrates a large language model (LLM) to provide players with an intelligent, interactive mission design advisor. Players can consult the AI for recommended spacecraft configurations based on their mission objectives, destination, budget, and engineering constraints. The system evaluates the requirements across all five major spacecraft subsystems—architecture, scientific instruments, power, communications, and launch vehicle—and recommends a configuration with detailed technical reasoning for each decision.

To ensure scientific credibility, the advisor uses retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to ground its recommendations in NASA and JPL mission documentation, spacecraft specifications, and engineering references. Rather than generating unsupported answers, the AI explains the trade-offs behind its recommendations and provides citations and direct links to relevant NASA sources, allowing players to independently verify the information and explore the underlying science.

This feature transforms the LLM from a conventional chatbot into an interactive engineering mentor. By comparing their own designs with AI-generated recommendations, players can develop a deeper understanding of systems engineering, technical decision-making, and the practical applications of artificial intelligence in aerospace. Our goal is to demonstrate how AI can make specialized scientific knowledge more accessible while encouraging critical thinking, evidence-based reasoning, and independent learning.

Scientific Validity and Technical Implementation

Scientific credibility was a primary consideration throughout development. The game's missions draw on publicly available information from NASA, the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, The Planetary Society, and published launch vehicle specifications.

Spacecraft costs, component masses, launch capacities, and mission requirements were simplified and rounded to maintain accessibility while preserving meaningful relationships between engineering variables.

The orbital mechanics visualization incorporates simplified circular-orbit assumptions and Hohmann transfer principles to introduce the physical considerations involved in interplanetary travel.

To maintain consistency, automated testing evaluates spacecraft configurations against the game's engineering rules, including budget limitations, mass constraints, power requirements, communication capabilities, and mission objectives.

Cosmic Command was developed using React, TypeScript, JavaScript, HTML, and CSS, with Vite as the build system. The application uses three.js for interactive 3D visualization and the Web Audio API for dynamically generated sound effects. The project is deployed through Vercel and operates directly in a modern web browser without requiring software installation, specialized hardware, or user accounts.

This technology stack was chosen to support interactive performance, ease of deployment, and broad accessibility across educational environments.

Mission Evaluation and Learning Through Failure

One of the project's central educational features is its post-launch evaluation system.

Following each launch attempt, the game assesses the spacecraft against eight engineering criteria and generates a detailed mission report identifying successful and unsuccessful subsystems.

Rather than presenting failure as a generic game-over screen, Cosmic Command explains the technical reasons behind each unsuccessful design. For example, an overweight spacecraft may fail to achieve the required trajectory, while a mission that exceeds its budget may be canceled before launch.

Players can review the evaluation, identify the decisions responsible for failure, and modify their spacecraft accordingly.

We designed this feedback system to reinforce the scientific method and the iterative nature of engineering. Real technological development frequently involves unsuccessful prototypes, unexpected constraints, and repeated refinement. Understanding why a design fails is often as important as achieving a successful result.

By making engineering failures understandable and actionable, the game encourages persistence, analytical reasoning, and evidence-based problem-solving.

The evaluation system also connects spacecraft designs to historical NASA missions, allowing players to explore real examples of the engineering concepts encountered during gameplay.

Creativity and Innovation

Cosmic Command's primary innovation is its integration of engineering decision-making into the core gameplay experience.

Unlike educational applications that separate instructional content from entertainment, the project's scientific concepts directly determine whether players succeed or fail. Engineering trade-offs are not supplemental lessons; they are the central challenge.

The combination of progressive mission objectives, interactive visualization, multidisciplinary engineering constraints, and detailed technical feedback creates a learning environment in which players develop understanding through experimentation.

Additional features, including adjustable mission parameters, shared spacecraft designs, instructor tools, and an answer-key system, extend the application's usefulness beyond individual gameplay. Educators can modify engineering constraints to demonstrate how changes in cost, mass, or launch capacity affect the feasibility of a mission.

The use of AI-assisted development also contributed to the project's technical scope, allowing us to integrate multiple interactive systems into a unified educational application.

Educational Impact and Global Relevance

Cosmic Command was designed to address the accessibility of engineering education by providing a free-to-access, browser-based environment in which students can explore aerospace concepts without specialized equipment or prior technical training.

Although the game focuses on spacecraft design, its educational value extends to technologies with direct applications on Earth.

Scientific instrumentation introduces the principles behind satellite-based environmental monitoring. Power system selection develops an understanding of energy generation and storage. Communication design demonstrates the importance of reliable connectivity, while launch vehicle selection and budgeting reinforce efficiency and resource optimization.

These concepts are relevant to challenges involving climate change, sustainable energy, disaster response, and global communications infrastructure.

The project also emphasizes broader engineering competencies, including requirements analysis, systems thinking, quantitative reasoning, collaboration, and iterative problem-solving.

By connecting the excitement of space exploration to technologies that benefit society, Cosmic Command aims to demonstrate that engineering is not simply about building sophisticated machines. It is about applying scientific knowledge to solve meaningful problems.

Relevance to the NASA Space Apps Challenge

Cosmic Command directly addresses the Space Mission Design Game challenge by providing an interactive environment in which players design robotic spacecraft, evaluate mission constraints, simulate launches, and analyze the results.

The project was developed around five priorities aligned with the NASA Space Apps judging criteria: meaningful educational impact, creative presentation, scientific credibility, relevance to the challenge, and technical usability.

Our objective was to create more than an entertaining game about space. We wanted to build an accessible introduction to the engineering process itself, allowing students to experience the same categories of decisions that shape real exploration missions.

By combining NASA-inspired science, AI-assisted software development, interactive simulations, and game-based learning, Cosmic Command demonstrates how emerging technologies can make complex scientific subjects more approachable.

Ultimately, our goal is to inspire the next generation of scientists, engineers, and innovators by showing that the skills used to explore other worlds are also the skills needed to solve important problems here on Earth.
